decks.title: Torque on a Current Loop — Part 1: Torque, magnetic moment and the loop as a dipole
goals: Derive the torque on a rectangular coil in a uniform field, τ = NIAB sin θ
Define the magnetic moment m = NIA and find its direction with the right-hand rule
Treat a current loop as a magnetic dipole and find the orbital magnetic moment of an electron in a Bohr orbit

slides.narration: Every electric motor, every analogue meter and every loudspeaker relies on one fact: a coil carrying a current in a magnetic field feels a turning effect. In this part we work out that torque for a rectangular coil, define the magnetic moment of a coil, see that a small current loop behaves exactly like a magnetic dipole, and apply the idea to an electron going round a nucleus.

slides.heading: Forces on the four sides of a coil
slides.body_md: A rectangular coil PQRS ($N$ turns, current $I$) can turn about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to a uniform field $\vec B$. Each side feels $\vec F = NI\,\vec l \times \vec B$.
bullets: QR and SP (length $l$) stay perpendicular to $\vec B$: forces $NIlB$, equal and opposite, on **different lines**: a couple.
PQ and RS (length $b$): equal and opposite forces along the **same line** (the axis): they cancel without turning.
Net force on the coil in a **uniform** field is zero.

slides.narration: Look at each side in turn. The two sides parallel to the axis always cut across the field, so each feels a force N I l B, one pushed out of the page and the other pushed in. The other two sides feel equal and opposite forces that act along the same line, so they cancel completely. The total force is zero, but the first pair forms a couple that turns the coil.

slides.heading: Deriving τ = NIAB sin θ
slides.body_md:
Seen from above, the two forces $F = NIlB$ act along parallel lines a distance $b\sin\theta$ apart, where $\theta$ is the angle between the normal to the coil and $\vec B$:
$$\tau = NIlB \times b\sin\theta = NIAB\sin\theta \qquad (A = lb)$$
bullets: The result holds for a flat coil of **any shape** of area $A$.
$\theta$ is measured from the **normal**, not from the plane of the coil.

slides.narration: Now look down on the coil from above. The two long sides appear as dots, one pushed up the page and one pushed down. The perpendicular distance between these two forces is b sine theta, where theta is the angle between the normal to the coil and the field. Torque is force times arm, N I l B times b sine theta, and since l times b is the area, the torque is N I A B sine theta.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: torque on a rectangular coil
slides.body_md: A coil of 120 turns, 5.0 cm × 3.0 cm, carries 0.40 A in a uniform field of 0.30 T. The axis of rotation is along the 5.0 cm sides and perpendicular to $\vec B$. Find (a) the force on each 5.0 cm side, (b) the largest torque, (c) the torque when the plane of the coil makes $60^\circ$ with the field.
bullets: (a) $F = NIlB = 120 \times 0.40 \times 0.050 \times 0.30 = 0.72$ N.
(b) Largest when the plane is along $\vec B$: $\tau_\text{max} = F \times b = 0.72 \times 0.030 = 0.0216$ N m.
(c) Plane at $60^\circ$ means the normal is at $\theta = 30^\circ$: $\tau = 0.0216 \times \sin 30^\circ = 0.0108$ N m.

slides.heading: Magnetic moment of a coil
slides.body_md:
Write the torque as $\tau = (NIA)B\sin\theta$. The **magnetic moment** of the coil is
$$\vec m = NI\vec A, \qquad \text{unit A m}^2$$
Its direction is along the normal given by the **right-hand rule**: curl the fingers of the right hand in the sense of the current; the thumb points along $\vec m$.
bullets: Anticlockwise current as seen: $\vec m$ towards you. Clockwise: away from you.
For a circular coil of radius $R$: $m = NI\pi R^2$.

slides.narration: The product N I A collects everything about the coil that matters for the torque, so we give it a name: the magnetic moment, measured in ampere square metres. It is a vector along the normal to the coil. To find which way, curl the fingers of your right hand round the coil in the direction of the current. Your thumb then points along the magnetic moment.

slides.heading: Torque as a vector: τ = m × B
slides.body_md:
$$\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B, \qquad \tau = mB\sin\theta$$
The torque always tends to turn $\vec m$ **into line with** $\vec B$.
bullets: At $\theta = 0^\circ$ a small twist produces a torque that brings the coil back: **stable**.
At $\theta = 180^\circ$ a small twist produces a torque that turns it further: **unstable**.

headers: Angle θ between m and B

visual.alt: Table of the torque on a coil at three orientations: zero and stable at 0 degrees, largest at 90 degrees, zero and unstable at 180 degrees

slides.narration: In vector form the torque is m cross B. It is zero when the moment is along the field or exactly opposite to it, and largest when the two are at right angles. The torque always tries to swing the moment round into line with the field. So the coil rests stably with m along B; with m opposite to B it is balanced, but the slightest nudge makes it flip over.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a circular coil in a field
slides.body_md: A flat circular coil of 40 turns and radius 5.0 cm lies in the plane of the page and carries 2.5 A anticlockwise as seen. A uniform field of 0.020 T points to the right, in the plane of the page. Find the magnetic moment and the torque, and describe how the coil turns.
bullets: $m = NI\pi R^2 = 40 \times 2.5 \times \pi \times (0.050)^2 \approx 0.785$ A m², **out of the page** (right-hand rule).
$\vec m \perp \vec B$, so $\tau = mB = 0.785 \times 0.020 \approx 0.016$ N m (the largest possible).
The torque turns the coil about the vertical line in the page through its centre until $\vec m$ points along $\vec B$, to the right.

slides.heading: A current loop is a magnetic dipole
slides.body_md:
Far from a small loop, its field has the same pattern as that of a short bar magnet or an electric dipole. On the axis at distance $x \gg R$:
$$B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{x^3}$$
(from the axial field of a loop, chapter 7, with $x \gg R$).
bullets: The face the moment points out of acts as a **north** face; the other as a **south** face.
The field falls as $1/x^3$, like that of any dipole.

visual.alt: Field lines of a current loop: a magnetic dipole

slides.narration: Step back from a small current loop and its field lines look just like those of a tiny bar magnet: they leave one face, loop round, and enter the other. The face that the magnetic moment points out of acts as a north pole. On the axis far away, the field is mu nought over four pi times two m over x cubed, falling off with the cube of the distance, like the field of any dipole.

slides.heading: Electric dipole and current loop compared
slides.body_md: The magnetic moment plays the role of the dipole moment:
columns:
**Electric dipole**
- Two charges ±q
- No net force in uniform E
- Turns to align p with E

**Current loop**
- A current round an area
- No net force in uniform B
- Turns to align m with B

rows: net force zero in a uniform field
net force zero in a uniform field

visual.alt: Table comparing an electric dipole in an electric field with a current loop in a magnetic field: moments p and m equal to N I A, no net force in a uniform field, torques p cross E and m cross B, and axial fields falling as the inverse cube of distance

slides.narration: Put the two side by side. An electric dipole in a uniform electric field feels no net force but a torque p cross E. A current loop in a uniform magnetic field feels no net force but a torque m cross B. Both settle with their moment along the field, and both have far fields that fall as the inverse cube of distance. One difference: there are no separate magnetic charges inside a loop.

slides.heading: The orbiting electron as a current loop
slides.body_md:
An electron (charge $-e$) moving at speed $v$ in a circle of radius $r$ is a current loop:
$$I = \dfrac{e}{T} = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}, \qquad \mu = I\pi r^2 = \dfrac{evr}{2}$$
With $L = m_evr$: $\mu = \dfrac{e}{2m_e}L$, and $\vec\mu$ is **opposite** to $\vec L$ because the charge is negative.
bullets: Bohr orbit: $L = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, so $\mu = n\dfrac{eh}{4\pi m_e}$.
**Bohr magneton** $\mu_B = \dfrac{eh}{4\pi m_e} \approx 9.27 \times 10^{-24}$ A m².

Multiply by the area of the orbit and the magnetic moment is e v r over two. Since the angular momentum is m v r, the moment is e over two m times L. Bohr’s rule fixes L as n h over two pi, so the moment comes in steps of the Bohr magneton.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the electron in hydrogen
slides.body_md: In the ground state of hydrogen the electron moves at $2.2 \times 10^{6}$ m s$^{-1}$ in an orbit of radius $5.3 \times 10^{-11}$ m. Find the equivalent current and the orbital magnetic moment.
bullets: $I = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2.2 \times 10^{6}}{2\pi \times 5.3 \times 10^{-11}} \approx 1.06 \times 10^{-3}$ A (about 1 mA).
$\mu = \dfrac{evr}{2} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2.2 \times 10^{6} \times 5.3 \times 10^{-11}}{2} \approx 9.33 \times 10^{-24}$ A m².
Compare $\mu_B \approx 9.27 \times 10^{-24}$ A m²: the ground state ($n = 1$) has one Bohr magneton, to the accuracy of the data.

slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Net force on a loop in uniform B
$\tau = NIAB\sin\theta$, θ between normal and B
$\vec m = NI\vec A$ (A m²), right-hand rule
$\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B$; stable at 0°, unstable at 180°

visual.alt: Summary table of the torque on a coil, its magnetic moment, the vector torque, the loop as a dipole and the orbital moment of the electron

slides.narration: To sum up: a coil in a uniform field feels no net force but a torque N I A B sine theta, where theta is measured from the normal. Its magnetic moment N I A points along the right-hand normal, and the torque m cross B turns it towards the field. A small loop is a magnetic dipole, and an orbiting electron has a magnetic moment e over two m times its angular momentum.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: In the derivation, show the forces on all four sides and say why two pairs behave differently.
Convert “plane at α to B” into θ = 90° − α before using sin θ.
Use the right-hand rule for the direction of m; no other rule is needed.
For the electron, μ is opposite to L: say why (negative charge).

visual.alt: Table of common questions and the key point for each

slides.narration: When you derive the torque, draw all four sides and explain why one pair of forces cancels and the other forms a couple. Watch the angle: if a question gives the angle between the plane and the field, subtract it from ninety degrees first. Use the right-hand rule for the moment. And for the electron, remember that its negative charge makes the moment opposite to its angular momentum.

slides.narration: The torque on a coil has a very practical use: the moving coil galvanometer, which can detect currents of a few microamperes. In this part we see how it is built and why its magnet has curved pole pieces, show that its deflection is proportional to the current, define its sensitivity, and then turn the same instrument into an ammeter and a voltmeter of any range we like.

slides.heading: Construction
slides.body_md: Main parts of a moving coil galvanometer:
bullets: A rectangular **coil** of many turns of fine insulated copper wire on a light frame, free to turn about a vertical axis.
A strong **magnet** with **concave** (cylindrical) pole pieces.
A **soft-iron cylinder** fixed inside the coil.
A **phosphor-bronze** suspension strip (or hairsprings) giving the restoring torque, with a mirror or pointer to read the deflection.

slides.narration: The heart of the instrument is a coil of many turns of fine copper wire, wound on a light frame and hung between the poles of a strong magnet. The pole pieces are curved, and a soft-iron cylinder sits inside the coil without touching it. A thin phosphor-bronze strip, or a pair of hairsprings, holds the coil, carries the current in and out, and twists back against any deflection.

slides.heading: Why a radial field?
slides.body_md:
The concave pole pieces and the soft-iron core make the field in the narrow gap **radial**. Whatever the deflection, the plane of the coil contains $\vec B$, so $\theta = 90^\circ$ and the deflecting torque is always
$$\tau = NIAB$$
bullets: The soft-iron core also **concentrates** the field lines, making $B$ larger and the galvanometer more sensitive.

slides.narration: Seen from above, the field lines in the gap all point along radii of the iron cylinder. As the coil turns, its sides move round inside this gap, and the field at each side still lies along the plane of the coil. So the angle between the moment and the field stays at ninety degrees, and the torque is simply N I A B at every deflection. The iron core also strengthens the field.

slides.heading: Principle and working: I = kθ
slides.body_md:
Principle: a coil carrying current in a magnetic field experiences a torque. The suspension twists back with a restoring torque $c\theta$ ($c$ = restoring torque per unit twist). The coil comes to rest when
$$NIAB = c\theta \;\Rightarrow\; I = \dfrac{c}{NAB}\,\theta = k\theta$$
bullets: $k = c/NAB$ is the **galvanometer constant**: current per unit deflection.
Since $I \propto \theta$, the scale is **evenly divided** (linear).

visual.alt: Current needed for a given deflection of a galvanometer coil: a straight line through the origin for a radial field, so the scale is evenly divided; a curve rising ever more steeply for a uniform field, which would crowd the scale divisions at large deflections
visual.caption: Only the radial field gives a linear scale.

slides.narration: When a current flows, the deflecting torque N I A B turns the coil, twisting the suspension. The suspension pushes back with a torque c theta that grows with the twist. The coil stops where the two balance, so the current equals c over N A B times the deflection. That constant, k, is the galvanometer constant. Because the current is proportional to the deflection, the scale divisions are evenly spaced.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: current for a given deflection
slides.body_md: A galvanometer coil has 60 turns, each 2.0 cm × 2.5 cm, in a radial field of 0.18 T. The restoring torque per unit twist is $4.5 \times 10^{-8}$ N m rad$^{-1}$. Find the current that deflects it by 0.30 rad, and its current sensitivity.
bullets: $I = \dfrac{c\theta}{NAB} = \dfrac{4.5 \times 10^{-8} \times 0.30}{5.4 \times 10^{-3}} = 2.5 \times 10^{-6}$ A, i.e. 2.5 μA.
Current sensitivity $\dfrac{\theta}{I} = \dfrac{NAB}{c} = 1.2 \times 10^{5}$ rad A$^{-1}$ (0.12 rad per μA).

slides.heading: Current and voltage sensitivity
slides.body_md: **Current sensitivity:** deflection per unit current, $\dfrac{\theta}{I} = \dfrac{NAB}{c}$. **Voltage sensitivity:** deflection per unit p.d. across the coil, $\dfrac{\theta}{V} = \dfrac{\theta}{IG} = \dfrac{NAB}{cG}$ ($G$ = coil resistance).
bullets: Raise sensitivity with more turns $N$, larger area $A$, stronger radial $B$ and a suspension of small $c$ (phosphor bronze).
More turns of the same wire also raise $G$, so the voltage sensitivity need not rise.

visual.alt: Table of the galvanometer constant, current sensitivity and voltage sensitivity with their expressions and units

slides.narration: A sensitive galvanometer gives a big deflection for a small current. Its current sensitivity is N A B over c. Its voltage sensitivity, the deflection per volt across the coil, is that divided by the coil resistance G. More turns, a larger coil, a stronger field or a weaker suspension all help. But adding turns also adds resistance, so the voltage sensitivity may not improve.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a divided scale
slides.body_md: A galvanometer of resistance 40 Ω has 30 divisions on its scale and gives full-scale deflection for 1.2 mA. Find its figure of merit (current per division), its current sensitivity and its voltage sensitivity.
bullets: $k = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{-3}}{30} = 4.0 \times 10^{-5}$ A per division (40 μA per division).
Current sensitivity $= \dfrac{30}{1.2\ \text{mA}} = 25$ divisions per mA.
Full-scale p.d. $= 1.2\ \text{mA} \times 40\ \Omega = 48$ mV; voltage sensitivity $= \dfrac{30}{48\ \text{mV}} \approx 0.625$ divisions per mV.

visual.alt: Table of the galvanometer constant, current sensitivity and voltage sensitivity with their expressions and units

slides.narration: Thirty divisions for one point two milliamperes means forty microamperes per division: that is the figure of merit. Turned round, the current sensitivity is twenty five divisions per milliampere. At full scale the coil carries one point two milliamperes through forty ohms, a potential difference of forty eight millivolts, so the voltage sensitivity is about point six two five division per millivolt.

slides.heading: Galvanometer to ammeter: the shunt
slides.body_md:
A galvanometer (resistance $G$, full-scale current $I_g$) reads up to $I$ when a small **shunt** $S$ is joined **in parallel**. Same p.d. across both: $I_gG = (I - I_g)S$, so
$$S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g}$$
bullets: If $I = nI_g$, then $S = \dfrac{G}{n - 1}$.
The ammeter’s resistance $\dfrac{GS}{G + S}$ is less than $S$: tiny, as an ammeter in series needs.

The coil and the shunt have the same potential difference, so I g times G equals the shunt current times S. slides.heading: Worked example 6: making an ammeter
slides.body_md: A galvanometer of resistance 24 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 2.5 mA. Find the shunt needed to make an ammeter of range 0–0.50 A, and the resistance of the ammeter.
bullets: $S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g} = \dfrac{2.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 24}{0.50 - 0.0025} = \dfrac{0.060}{0.4975} \approx 0.121$ Ω, in parallel.
Ammeter resistance $= \dfrac{24 \times 0.121}{24 + 0.121} \approx 0.120$ Ω.

slides.heading: Galvanometer to voltmeter: the series resistance
slides.body_md:
For a voltmeter of range $V$, a large resistance $R$ is joined **in series** so that $I_g$ flows when $V$ is applied: $V = I_g(G + R)$, so
$$R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G$$
bullets: A tap between series resistors gives a **multi-range** voltmeter.
The voltmeter’s resistance $G + R$ is large, as a meter in parallel needs.

slides.heading: Meters in real circuits
slides.body_md: A real meter changes what it measures. Example: 6.0 V across 1.0 kΩ and 2.0 kΩ in series puts 4.0 V across the 2.0 kΩ resistor; a 2.0 kΩ voltmeter placed across it makes that part $1.0$ kΩ and reads only $3.0$ V.
bullets: A voltmeter should have a resistance **much larger** than the resistance it is across.
An ammeter should have a resistance **much smaller** than the rest of the circuit.

visual.alt: Reading of a voltmeter placed across the 2 kilo-ohm resistor of a 1 kilo-ohm and 2 kilo-ohm divider on 6 volts, against the voltmeter resistance: 3 volts for a 2 kilo-ohm meter, rising towards the true 4 volts as the meter resistance becomes large
visual.caption: A good voltmeter has a resistance much larger than the resistance it is connected across.

slides.narration: Meters are not perfect. Take six volts across one kilo-ohm and two kilo-ohms in series: the two kilo-ohm resistor has four volts across it. A voltmeter of only two kilo-ohms in parallel turns that part of the circuit into one kilo-ohm, and it reads just three volts. As the graph shows, the reading approaches four volts only when the meter’s resistance is many times larger.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 2
slides.body_md: Key results:
bullets: Radial field: torque $NIAB$ at every angle; $I = k\theta$, $k = c/NAB$, a linear scale.
Current sensitivity $NAB/c$; voltage sensitivity $NAB/cG$.
Ammeter: shunt $S = I_gG/(I - I_g)$ in parallel. Voltmeter: $R = V/I_g - G$ in series.

visual.alt: Table comparing ammeter and voltmeter: an ammeter has a small shunt in parallel, goes in series and ideally has zero resistance; a voltmeter has a large series resistance, goes in parallel and ideally has infinite resistance

slides.narration: To sum up: the galvanometer’s radial field keeps the torque at N I A B, so the current is proportional to the deflection. Its current sensitivity is N A B over c, and its voltage sensitivity is that divided by the coil resistance. A small shunt in parallel makes it an ammeter of low resistance; a large resistance in series makes it a voltmeter of high resistance.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: Explain the radial field in terms of the angle between the plane of the coil and B.
Shunt: equate the p.d. across coil and shunt. Voltmeter: total resistance = V/Ig.
Work in amperes and ohms; convert mA and μA first.
When asked to compare sensitivities, check whether G changes too.

visual.alt: Table of common questions and the key point for each

slides.narration: For the radial field, say that the plane of the coil always contains the field, so the torque is the same at every angle. For a shunt, set the potential difference across the coil equal to that across the shunt; for a voltmeter, find the total resistance first. Convert milliamperes and microamperes to amperes before you substitute, and check whether the coil resistance changes when comparing sensitivities.

notes.title: Torque on a Current Loop and the Moving Coil Galvanometer — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Torque on a rectangular coil
sections.body_md:
- Coil PQRS of N turns, current I, free to turn about an axis perpendicular to a uniform field B. Each side feels $\vec F = NI\,\vec l \times \vec B$.
- The two sides parallel to the axis (length l) feel forces NIlB, equal and opposite on different lines: a **couple**. The other two sides feel equal, opposite, **collinear** forces: no torque. **Net force = 0** in a uniform field.
- Arm of the couple $= b\sin\theta$ (θ between the **normal** and B): $\tau = NIlB \cdot b\sin\theta = NIAB\sin\theta$, true for a flat coil of any shape.
- Largest ($NIAB$) when the plane of the coil is along B; zero when the plane is perpendicular to B.

key_terms.definition_md: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces on different lines: no net force, but a torque equal to one force times the distance between the lines.

sections.heading: 2. Magnetic moment and the vector torque
sections.body_md:
- **Magnetic moment** $\vec m = NI\vec A$ (A m²), along the normal given by the **right-hand rule**: fingers curled along the current, thumb along $\vec m$. Circular coil: $m = NI\pi R^2$.
- $\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B$: the torque turns $\vec m$ towards $\vec B$. θ = 0°: zero torque, **stable**; θ = 90°: largest torque; θ = 180°: zero torque, **unstable**.
- If the plane of the coil makes angle α with B, then θ = 90° − α.

key_terms.definition_md: NIA, a vector along the right-hand normal to the coil; unit A m².

sections.heading: 3. Current loop as a magnetic dipole; the orbiting electron
sections.body_md:
- A small current loop behaves as a **magnetic dipole**: field lines like those of a short bar magnet; the face $\vec m$ points out of is a north face. Far away on the axis $B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{x^3}$ (compare $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2p}{x^3}$ for an electric dipole). In a uniform field: no net force, torque $\vec m \times \vec B$.
- Electron in a circular orbit (Bohr model): $I = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}$, $\mu = I\pi r^2 = \dfrac{evr}{2} = \dfrac{e}{2m_e}L$; $\vec\mu$ is **opposite** to $\vec L$ (negative charge). Gyromagnetic ratio $\dfrac{e}{2m_e} \approx 8.8 \times 10^{10}$ C kg⁻¹.
- Bohr orbit $L = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$: $\mu = n\mu_B$, **Bohr magneton** $\mu_B = \dfrac{eh}{4\pi m_e} \approx 9.27 \times 10^{-24}$ A m².

key_terms.definition_md: Orbital magnetic moment of the electron in the first Bohr orbit, eh/4πmₑ ≈ 9.27 × 10⁻²⁴ A m².
Ratio of orbital magnetic moment to orbital angular momentum, e/2mₑ for an electron.

sections.heading: 4. Moving coil galvanometer
sections.body_md:
- **Construction:** coil of many turns of fine insulated wire on a light frame; strong magnet with **concave** pole pieces; **soft-iron** cylinder inside the coil; phosphor-bronze suspension (or hairsprings) giving the restoring torque; mirror and lamp-and-scale, or a pointer.
- **Principle:** a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a torque.
- **Radial field:** the plane of the coil always contains B, so the deflecting torque is $NIAB$ at every deflection. The soft iron also makes B stronger.
- **Working:** $NIAB = c\theta \Rightarrow I = \dfrac{c}{NAB}\theta = k\theta$ ($c$ = restoring torque per unit twist, $k$ = galvanometer constant): a **linear scale**.
- **Current sensitivity** $\dfrac{\theta}{I} = \dfrac{NAB}{c}$; **voltage sensitivity** $\dfrac{\theta}{V} = \dfrac{NAB}{cG}$. More turns raise both N and G.

key_terms.definition_md: Field directed along radii of the soft-iron core, so the plane of the coil always contains B.
Deflection per unit p.d. across the coil, NAB/cG.

sections.heading: 5. Ammeter and voltmeter from a galvanometer
sections.body_md:
- **Ammeter** of range I: shunt in **parallel**, $I_gG = (I - I_g)S \Rightarrow S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g}$; for $I = nI_g$, $S = \dfrac{G}{n - 1}$. Resistance $\dfrac{GS}{G + S}$ (very small); connected in series.
- **Voltmeter** of range V: resistance in **series**, $V = I_g(G + R) \Rightarrow R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G$. Resistance $G + R$ (very large); connected in parallel. Taps give several ranges.
- Ideal ammeter: zero resistance; ideal voltmeter: infinite resistance. A real voltmeter across a resistor comparable with its own resistance reads low.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A flat coil carrying a current in a uniform magnetic field experiences a torque NIAB sin θ whatever its shape, A being the area the coil encloses.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The torque depends only on the magnetic moment NIA (and the angle), so circular, square or irregular flat coils of the same area behave alike.

questions.stem_md: A rectangular coil carrying a steady current hangs in a uniform magnetic field and can turn about a vertical axis perpendicular to the field. The torque on it is greatest when the angle between the field and the plane of the coil is
questions.solution_md: With the plane along the field, the normal is perpendicular to B, so θ = 90° and sin θ = 1: the torque NIAB is the largest — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A rectangular coil of 30 turns, 8.0 cm × 5.0 cm, carries 1.2 A in a uniform field of 0.25 T. The plane of the coil makes 30° with the field. Find the torque on the coil, in units of 10⁻² N m (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: The normal makes $\theta = 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$ with $\vec B$. $\tau = NIAB\sin\theta = 30 \times 1.2 \times (0.080 \times 0.050) \times 0.25 \times \sin 60^\circ \approx 0.0312$ N m, i.e. $0.0312 \times 10^{2} = 3.12$.

questions.stem_md: A flat circular coil of 250 turns and diameter 6.0 cm carries a current of 80 mA. Find its magnetic moment, in units of 10⁻² A m² (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Radius $= 0.030$ m. $m = NI\pi R^2 = 250 \times 0.080 \times \pi \times (0.030)^2 \approx 0.0565$ A m², i.e. $0.0565 \times 10^{2} = 5.65$.

marking_scheme.step: m = NIπR² with R = 3.0 cm: 5.65 × 10⁻² A m²

questions.stem_md: A coil of magnetic moment 0.45 A m² experiences a largest possible torque of 0.054 N m in a uniform magnetic field. Find the magnetic field, in tesla.
questions.solution_md: The largest torque is $mB$, so $B = \dfrac{\tau_\text{max}}{m} = \dfrac{0.054}{0.45} = 0.12$ T.

questions.stem_md: A coil of 60 turns, each of area 40 cm², carries 0.50 A in a uniform field of 0.30 T and experiences a torque of 0.0216 N m. Find the angle between the normal to the coil and the field, in degrees (to the nearest degree).
questions.solution_md: $m = NIA = 60 \times 0.50 \times 40 \times 10^{-4} = 0.12$ A m², so $mB = 0.12 \times 0.30 = 0.036$ N m. $\sin\theta = \dfrac{0.0216}{0.036} = 0.60$, so $\theta = 36.9$ degrees, i.e. 37 degrees to the nearest degree (the plane of the coil is then at about 53 degrees to the field).

questions.stem_md: A flat circular coil lies on a horizontal table. Seen from above, the current in it flows clockwise. Its magnetic moment points

options.text_md: vertically upwards, away from the table
vertically downwards, into the table
horizontally, along a diameter of the coil
along the wire, in the direction of the current

questions.solution_md: Curl the fingers of the right hand clockwise as seen from above: the thumb points down, into the table — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A current-carrying coil that is free to turn in a uniform magnetic field comes to rest with its magnetic moment pointing along the field.

**Reason (R):** The torque m × B always acts to turn the magnetic moment of the coil towards the direction of the field.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: the torque swings m towards B, and the only stable position is m along B, where the torque is zero — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Show that a rectangular current-carrying coil placed in a uniform magnetic field experiences no net force, although it may experience a torque.

answer.model_answer_md: Opposite sides of the coil have **equal lengths** and carry the current in **opposite directions**, so in a uniform field the forces on them are **equal and opposite**: the four forces add to **zero**. The forces on the two sides parallel to the axis act along **different lines**, so they form a **couple**, which turns the coil.

questions.solution_md: Equal and opposite forces; couple from non-collinear pair.

marking_scheme.step: Forces on opposite sides equal and opposite: net force zero
One pair not collinear: a couple (torque)

questions.stem_md: A rectangular coil of N turns has sides of length l, parallel to its axis of rotation, and b. It carries current I in a uniform field B perpendicular to the axis, its normal making angle θ with B. Starting from the force on each side, derive the torque on the coil and write it in vector form.

answer.model_answer_md: The sides of length $l$ stay perpendicular to $\vec B$; each feels $F = NIlB$, the two forces being equal, opposite and parallel. The sides of length $b$ feel equal and opposite forces along the axis, which cancel and give no torque. The perpendicular distance between the lines of the two forces $NIlB$ is $b\sin\theta$, so they form a couple of moment $\tau = NIlB \cdot b\sin\theta = NIAB\sin\theta$, with $A = lb$. With $\vec m = NI\vec A$ along the right-hand normal, $\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B$.

questions.solution_md: Couple of the two forces NIlB with arm b sin θ.

marking_scheme.step: F = NIlB on the sides of length l; other pair cancels
τ = NIAB sin θ and τ = m × B

questions.stem_md: A fixed length of wire carrying a current I is bent into a flat circular coil of one turn. It is then rewound into a flat circular coil of two turns, with the same current. Compared with the one-turn coil, the magnetic moment of the two-turn coil is

options.text_md: twice as large
the same
one quarter as large
half as large

questions.solution_md: With length $L$ and $n$ turns, the radius is $L/2\pi n$, so $m = nI\pi\left(\dfrac{L}{2\pi n}\right)^2 = \dfrac{IL^2}{4\pi n}$. Doubling $n$ halves $m$: the area falls to a quarter while the turns only double — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A single square loop of side 10 cm carries 4.0 A in a uniform field of 0.15 T. Find the largest torque it can experience, in mN m.
questions.solution_md: $\tau_\text{max} = IAB = 4.0 \times (0.10)^2 \times 0.15 = 6.0 \times 10^{-3}$ N m, i.e. $6.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{3} = 6.0$ mN m, when the plane of the loop is along the field.

questions.stem_md: A current loop in a uniform magnetic field is balanced with its magnetic moment pointing exactly opposite to the field. It is turned through a small angle and released. It

options.text_md: returns to its original position, because the torque now opposes the displacement
stays at its new angle, because the torque is still zero there
moves bodily along the field, because a net force now acts on it
turns further away and swings round towards the position with m along B

questions.solution_md: At θ = 180° the torque is zero, but for a small displacement $\vec m \times \vec B$ turns m further from its starting direction, towards B: the equilibrium is unstable. A uniform field gives no net force — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In τ = NIAB sin θ for a rectangular coil turning in a magnetic field, the angle θ is measured between the field and the ___ to the plane of the coil.
questions.solution_md: The **normal** to the plane of the coil (the direction of its magnetic moment).

questions.stem_md: A flat coil lies in the xy-plane and its current circulates anticlockwise when viewed from the +z side. A uniform magnetic field points along +x. The torque on the coil points along

options.text_md: −y
+y
+z
−x

questions.solution_md: By the right-hand rule $\vec m$ is along $+z$. $\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B \propto \hat z \times \hat x = \hat y$: the torque is along $+y$, turning $\vec m$ towards $+x$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A rectangular coil of 50 turns, 3.0 cm × 2.0 cm, is placed in a uniform field of 0.40 T. What current must it carry so that the largest torque on it is 1.2 × 10⁻³ N m? Give the answer in amperes.
questions.solution_md: $\tau_\text{max} = NIAB$, so $I = \dfrac{\tau_\text{max}}{NAB} = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{-3}}{50 \times 6.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.40} = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{-3}}{0.012} = 0.10$ A.

questions.stem_md: A circular coil of 25 turns and radius 4.0 cm carries 3.0 A in a uniform field of 0.050 T. Find (a) its magnetic moment, (b) the torque on it when the plane of the coil is along the field, (c) the torque when the plane of the coil makes 60° with the field.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $m = NI\pi R^2 = 25 \times 3.0 \times \pi \times (0.040)^2 \approx 0.377$ A m².
(b) Plane along $\vec B$: normal at $90^\circ$, $\tau = mB = 0.377 \times 0.050 \approx 0.0188$ N m (the largest).
(c) Plane at $60^\circ$: normal at $\theta = 30^\circ$, $\tau = mB\sin 30^\circ \approx 9.42 \times 10^{-3}$ N m.

questions.solution_md: m = NIπR²; τ = mB sin θ with θ from the normal.

questions.stem_md: A student proposes to lift a small iron weight by hanging it from a current-carrying coil placed in the uniform field between two large magnet poles, arguing that the field pushes on the coil. Evaluate the proposal.

answer.model_answer_md: It will **not work**. In a **uniform** field the forces on opposite sides of the coil are equal and opposite, so the **net force is zero**; the coil only feels a **torque** that turns it until its moment lies along the field. A net force needs a **non-uniform** field.

questions.solution_md: No net force in a uniform field; only a torque.

marking_scheme.step: Net force zero in a uniform field
Only a torque that aligns m with B

questions.stem_md: Looking at one face of a flat circular loop, you see the current flowing anticlockwise. That face of the loop behaves like

options.text_md: the south pole of a magnet
the north pole of a magnet
a region where the field is zero
neither pole, since a single loop has no poles

questions.solution_md: By the right-hand rule the moment m points towards you; field lines emerge from the face that m points out of, as from a north pole — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The field on the axis of a circular loop of radius $R$ carrying current $I$, at distance $x$ from its centre, is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0IR^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$. Show that far from the loop $B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{x^3}$, and state what this shows about the loop.

answer.model_answer_md: For $x \gg R$, $(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2} \approx x^3$, so $B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0IR^2}{2x^3} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2I(\pi R^2)}{x^3} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{x^3}$ with $m = I\pi R^2$. This has the same form as the axial field of an electric dipole, $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2p}{x^3}$: the loop behaves as a **magnetic dipole** of moment m.

questions.solution_md: Neglect R² beside x²; write IπR² as m.

questions.stem_md: The magnetic field on the axis of a small current loop, far from it at a distance x, is B. At a distance 2x along the same axis, the field is
questions.solution_md: Far from a magnetic dipole the axial field varies as 1/x³; doubling x divides B by 2³ = 8 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A small coil of magnetic moment 0.50 A m² is treated as a magnetic dipole. Find the magnetic field on its axis at a distance of 40 cm from it, in μT (3 significant figures).

**Assertion (A):** A small current loop placed in a uniform magnetic field experiences no net force.

**Reason (R):** The magnetic forces on opposite sides of such a loop always act along the same line, so they cannot produce a torque either.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the forces on opposite sides cancel in a uniform field. R is false: one pair of forces generally acts along different lines and forms a couple, so the loop feels a torque m × B, just as an electric dipole does in a uniform E — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why a small plane loop carrying a current is described as a magnetic dipole.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Far from the loop its field lines have the **same pattern** as those of a short bar magnet, emerging from one face (north) and entering the other (south), with an axial field $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{x^3}$. (ii) In a **uniform field** it feels **no net force** but a **torque** $\vec m \times \vec B$ that aligns m with B, exactly like a bar magnet.

questions.solution_md: Dipole field pattern; torque without net force.

marking_scheme.step: Field pattern of a dipole (1/x³, N and S faces)
Torque m × B with no net force in uniform B

questions.stem_md: In the second Bohr orbit of hydrogen, the electron moves at about 1.1 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ in a circle of radius 2.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Find the equivalent current of the orbiting electron, in mA (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: One charge $e$ passes any point of the orbit once per period: $I = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.1 \times 10^{6}}{2\pi \times 2.1 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 1.33 \times 10^{-4}$ A, i.e. $1.33 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{3} = 0.133$ mA.

questions.stem_md: For the same electron (speed 1.1 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, orbit radius 2.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m), find the orbital magnetic moment, in units of 10⁻²³ A m² (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\mu = \dfrac{evr}{2} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.1 \times 10^{6} \times 2.1 \times 10^{-10}}{2} \approx 1.85 \times 10^{-23}$ A m², i.e. $\dfrac{1.85 \times 10^{-23}}{10^{-23}} = 1.85$ (about two Bohr magnetons, as expected for n = 2).

questions.stem_md: Using e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, calculate the Bohr magneton, in units of 10⁻²⁴ A m² (3 significant figures).
For an electron moving in a circular orbit, the ratio of its orbital magnetic moment to its orbital angular momentum

options.text_md: is e/mₑ, the same for every orbit
increases with the radius of the orbit
is e/2mₑ, the same for every orbit
decreases as the speed of the electron increases

questions.solution_md: μ = evr/2 and L = mₑvr, so μ/L = e/2mₑ: v and r cancel — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The orbital magnetic moment of an electron in an atom points opposite to its orbital angular momentum.

**Reason (R):** The electron is negatively charged, so the conventional current of its orbit circulates opposite to its motion.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: L follows the motion, μ follows the conventional current, which is reversed for a negative charge — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the Bohr model, the orbital magnetic moment of the electron in hydrogen can take only whole-number multiples of the Bohr magneton.

**Reason (R):** The electron in a hydrogen atom carries a charge of magnitude 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A: μ is quantised because μ = (e/2mₑ)L and Bohr’s condition makes L = nh/2π, giving μ = nμB — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Find the ratio of the orbital magnetic moment to the orbital angular momentum of an electron (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg), in units of 10¹⁰ C kg⁻¹ (3 significant figures).
In which Bohr orbit of hydrogen does the electron have an orbital magnetic moment of 2.78 × 10⁻²³ A m²? (Take the Bohr magneton as 9.27 × 10⁻²⁴ A m².)
questions.solution_md: $\mu = n\mu_B$, so $n = \dfrac{2.78 \times 10^{-23}}{9.27 \times 10^{-24}} = 3$ (the third orbit).

questions.stem_md: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, the orbit radius varies as n² and the speed of the electron as 1/n. How do the equivalent current I of the orbit and the orbital magnetic moment μ vary with n?

options.text_md: I ∝ 1/n and μ ∝ n²
I ∝ n and μ ∝ n³
I ∝ 1/n³ and μ ∝ n
I ∝ 1/n³ and μ ∝ 1/n

questions.solution_md: I = ev/2πr ∝ (1/n)/n² = 1/n³; μ = evr/2 ∝ (1/n)(n²) = n, in step with μ = nμB — option (c).

questions.stem_md: An electron of mass mₑ and charge −e moves with speed v in a circular orbit of radius r. Show that its orbital magnetic moment is μ = (e/2mₑ)L, where L is its orbital angular momentum, and use Bohr’s quantum condition to obtain the Bohr magneton.

answer.model_answer_md: The period is $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v}$, so the orbit is a current $I = \dfrac{e}{T} = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}$ round an area $\pi r^2$. Its moment is $\mu = I\pi r^2 = \dfrac{evr}{2}$. Since $L = m_evr$, $\mu = \dfrac{e}{2m_e}L$; $\vec\mu$ is opposite to $\vec L$ because the charge is negative. Bohr’s condition $L = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$ gives $\mu = n\dfrac{eh}{4\pi m_e}$; for $n = 1$ this is the Bohr magneton $\mu_B = \dfrac{eh}{4\pi m_e} \approx 9.27 \times 10^{-24}$ A m².

questions.solution_md: Current e/T times area; L = mₑvr; L = nh/2π.

questions.stem_md: An electron revolves in a circular orbit of radius 8.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m, making 3.0 × 10¹⁵ revolutions per second. Find (a) the equivalent current, (b) its orbital magnetic moment, (c) its orbital angular momentum, and verify that the ratio of (b) to (c) is e/2mₑ.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $I = ef = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 3.0 \times 10^{15} = 4.8 \times 10^{-4}$ A.
(b) $\mu = I\pi r^2 = 4.8 \times 10^{-4} \times \pi \times (8.0 \times 10^{-11})^2 \approx 9.65 \times 10^{-24}$ A m².
(c) $v = 2\pi rf$, so $L = m_evr = 2\pi m_efr^2 \approx 1.10 \times 10^{-34}$ kg m² s$^{-1}$.
Ratio $\dfrac{\mu}{L} \approx 8.79 \times 10^{10}$ C kg$^{-1}$, equal to $\dfrac{e}{2m_e} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{1.82 \times 10^{-30}} \approx 8.79 \times 10^{10}$ C kg$^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: I = ef; μ = Iπr²; L = mₑvr.

marking_scheme.step: L ≈ 1.10 × 10⁻³⁴ kg m² s⁻¹; ratio 8.79 × 10¹⁰ C kg⁻¹

questions.stem_md: The moving coil galvanometer works on the principle that

options.text_md: a coil carrying a current in a magnetic field experiences a torque
a changing magnetic flux through a coil induces an emf in it
a current-carrying wire sets up a magnetic field around itself
like magnetic poles repel and unlike poles attract

questions.solution_md: The deflecting torque NIAB on the coil, balanced by the restoring torque of the suspension, measures the current — option (a).

questions.stem_md: As the coil of a moving coil galvanometer turns in the radial field between its pole pieces, the plane of the coil

options.text_md: always contains the field lines at the coil sides, so sin θ stays equal to 1
stays perpendicular to the field lines, so the torque stays zero until the spring acts
turns away from the field lines, so the torque falls as the deflection grows
cuts the field lines at 45°, so the torque is NIAB/√2

questions.solution_md: In a radial field the field at each coil side lies along a radius, which is in the plane of the coil at every deflection: the normal stays at 90° to B and the torque stays NIAB — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The suspension strip of a sensitive moving coil galvanometer is made of phosphor bronze.

**Reason (R):** Phosphor bronze has a small restoring torque per unit twist and returns fully to its original state after being twisted.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: a small c gives a large deflection for a small current (current sensitivity NAB/c), and full recovery keeps the zero steady — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Winding more turns of the same wire on a galvanometer coil always increases its voltage sensitivity.

**Reason (R):** The current sensitivity of a galvanometer is directly proportional to the number of turns on its coil.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true: θ/I = NAB/c. A is false: more turns of the same wire raise the coil resistance G in proportion, so the voltage sensitivity NAB/cG need not increase — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer coil of 80 turns, each 2.0 cm × 1.5 cm, turns in a radial field of 0.25 T against a suspension whose restoring torque is 6.0 × 10⁻⁸ N m per radian. Find the deflection produced by a current of 2.0 μA, in radians.
questions.solution_md: $NIAB = c\theta$: $\theta = \dfrac{NIAB}{c} = \dfrac{80 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 3.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.25}{6.0 \times 10^{-8}} = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{-8}}{6.0 \times 10^{-8}} = 0.20$ rad.

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer has a coil of 150 turns, each of area 1.2 cm², in a radial field of 0.40 T. The restoring torque per unit twist is 1.8 × 10⁻⁷ N m rad⁻¹ and the coil resistance is 80 Ω. Find its voltage sensitivity, in radians per millivolt.
questions.solution_md: Current sensitivity $\dfrac{NAB}{c} = \dfrac{150 \times 1.2 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.40}{1.8 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.0 \times 10^{4}$ rad A$^{-1}$. Voltage sensitivity $= \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{4}}{80} = 500$ rad V$^{-1}$, i.e. $\dfrac{500}{1000} = 0.50$ rad per mV.

marking_scheme.step: Divide by G: 0.50 rad per mV

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer has 25 divisions on each side of its zero and gives full-scale deflection for 0.50 mA. Find its figure of merit (current per division), in μA per division.
questions.solution_md: $k = \dfrac{0.50\ \text{mA}}{25} = \dfrac{500}{25} = 20$ μA per division.

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer coil of 100 turns, each of area 4.0 cm², is in a radial field of 0.20 T. A current of 0.50 mA turns it through 90°. Find the restoring torque per unit twist of its suspension, in units of 10⁻⁶ N m rad⁻¹ (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $90^\circ = \pi/2$ rad. $c = \dfrac{NIAB}{\theta} = \dfrac{100 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.20}{\pi/2} = \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-6}}{1.571} \approx 2.55 \times 10^{-6}$ N m rad$^{-1}$, i.e. $\dfrac{2.55 \times 10^{-6}}{10^{-6}} = 2.55$.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the concave pole pieces and the soft-iron core of a moving coil galvanometer together make its scale evenly divided.

answer.model_answer_md: Together they make the field in the narrow gap **radial**, along radii of the core. The coil sides move round inside this gap, so the plane of the coil **always contains B** and the deflecting torque is **NIAB at every angle**. Balancing it against the restoring torque cθ gives **θ ∝ I**, so equal steps of current give equal deflections.

questions.solution_md: Radial field keeps the torque NIAB, so θ ∝ I.

marking_scheme.step: Radial field: plane of coil always along B, torque NIAB
NIAB = cθ gives θ ∝ I: even scale

questions.stem_md: State two ways of increasing the current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer, and a practical drawback of each.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **More turns** on the coil: the coil becomes heavier and its **resistance rises**, so the voltage sensitivity may not improve. (ii) A **weaker suspension** (smaller c, e.g. a thinner strip): the coil becomes **fragile** and slow to settle, and the zero can drift. (A stronger magnet or a larger coil also helps, but makes the instrument bulky.)

questions.solution_md: NAB/c: raise N, A, B or lower c.

marking_scheme.step: Two valid ways (N, A, B up or c down)

questions.stem_md: Explain the working of a moving coil galvanometer and show that the current through it is proportional to the deflection of its coil. Name the constant of proportionality.

answer.model_answer_md: When a current $I$ flows, the coil in the **radial field** feels a deflecting torque $NIAB$ (the plane of the coil always contains $\vec B$). The coil turns and twists the suspension, which sets up a **restoring torque** $c\theta$ proportional to the deflection. The coil comes to rest when $NIAB = c\theta$, so $I = \dfrac{c}{NAB}\theta = k\theta$: the current is **proportional** to the deflection. $k = c/NAB$ is the **galvanometer constant**.

questions.solution_md: Deflecting torque NIAB balanced by cθ.

marking_scheme.step: Deflecting torque NIAB in a radial field
I = kθ, k = c/NAB the galvanometer constant

questions.stem_md: Define the current sensitivity and the voltage sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer and obtain expressions for them. Explain why winding more turns of the same wire on the coil need not increase its voltage sensitivity.

answer.model_answer_md: **Current sensitivity** is the deflection per unit current: from $NIAB = c\theta$, $\dfrac{\theta}{I} = \dfrac{NAB}{c}$. **Voltage sensitivity** is the deflection per unit potential difference across the coil: with $V = IG$, $\dfrac{\theta}{V} = \dfrac{NAB}{cG}$. Doubling N with the same wire doubles the length of wire and so doubles G as well; $N/G$ is unchanged, so the voltage sensitivity stays the same although the current sensitivity doubles.

questions.solution_md: θ/I = NAB/c; θ/V = NAB/cG; G ∝ N.

marking_scheme.step: G rises with N, so N/G unchanged

questions.stem_md: Which one of these changes would NOT increase the current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer?

options.text_md: Using a stronger permanent magnet
Increasing the area of the coil
Winding more turns on the coil
Using a suspension with a larger restoring torque per unit twist

questions.solution_md: Current sensitivity NAB/c rises with N, A and B but falls as c increases — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Match each galvanometer part in Column A with its role in Column B.

options.text_md: Concave pole pieces
Soft-iron cylinder inside the coil
Phosphor-bronze strip
Small mirror on the suspension

match_right.text_md: Concentrates the field lines, increasing B in the gap
Reflects a light beam onto a scale to show small deflections
Shapes the field in the gap so that it is radial
Provides the restoring torque and leads current into the coil

questions.solution_md: Pole pieces → radial field (1 → r); soft iron → stronger B (2 → p); strip → restoring torque and current lead (3 → s); mirror → lamp-and-scale reading (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: Suppose the radial field of a galvanometer were replaced by a uniform field, with the plane of the coil along the field at zero deflection. The current needed to produce a deflection φ would then be proportional to

options.text_md: φ
φ / cos φ
φ cos φ
sin φ

questions.solution_md: After turning through φ the normal makes 90° − φ with B, so the deflecting torque is NIAB cos φ. Balancing cφ gives I ∝ φ/cos φ: the scale would be crowded at large deflections — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Doubling the number of turns on a galvanometer coil, everything else unchanged, doubles both its current sensitivity and its figure of merit (current per division).

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The current sensitivity NAB/c doubles, but the figure of merit k = c/NAB is its reciprocal, so it is halved.

questions.stem_md: In the relation I = kθ for a moving coil galvanometer, the constant k, equal to c/NAB, is called the ___ constant.
questions.solution_md: The **galvanometer** constant (current per unit deflection).

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer has a coil of resistance 60 Ω and a scale of 50 divisions; a current of 15 μA deflects it by one division. Find (a) the current for full-scale deflection, (b) its current sensitivity in divisions per mA, (c) its voltage sensitivity in divisions per mV.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $I_g = 50 \times 15\ \mu\text{A} = 0.75$ mA.
(b) One division per 15 μA: $\dfrac{1}{0.015\ \text{mA}} \approx 66.7$ divisions per mA.
(c) One division needs $15 \times 10^{-6} \times 60 = 9.0 \times 10^{-4}$ V $= 0.90$ mV, so the voltage sensitivity is $\dfrac{1}{0.90} \approx 1.11$ divisions per mV.

questions.solution_md: Ig = nk; reciprocal of current and of voltage per division.

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer of resistance G is to be converted into an ammeter whose range is n times the galvanometer’s full-scale current. The shunt required is

options.text_md: G/n
nG

questions.solution_md: IgG = (I − Ig)S with I = nIg gives S = G/(n − 1) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer of resistance 25 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 4.0 mA. Find the shunt needed to convert it into an ammeter of range 0–5.0 A, in ohms (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g} = \dfrac{0.0040 \times 25}{5.0 - 0.0040} = \dfrac{0.10}{4.996} \approx 0.0200$ Ω, connected in parallel.

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer of resistance 75 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 1.5 mA. Find the resistance to be connected in series with it to make a voltmeter of range 0–30 V, in ohms.
questions.solution_md: Total resistance $= \dfrac{V}{I_g} = \dfrac{30}{1.5 \times 10^{-3}} = 20000$ Ω; $R = 20000 - 75 = 19925$ Ω, in series.

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer of resistance 120 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 2.5 mA. A shunt of 0.30 Ω is connected across it. Find the range of the ammeter so formed, in amperes (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: At full scale the p.d. across the coil is $I_gG = 0.0025 \times 120 = 0.30$ V. The shunt then carries $\dfrac{0.30}{0.30} = 1.0$ A, so $I = 0.0025 + 1.0 = 1.00$ A.

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer of resistance 15 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 10 mA. A 485 Ω resistor is connected in series with it. Find the range of the voltmeter so formed, in volts.
An ammeter of resistance 0.10 Ω reads up to 1.0 A. What shunt must be connected across it to make it read up to 5.0 A? Give the answer in ohms.
questions.solution_md: Treat the ammeter as a meter of resistance 0.10 Ω and full-scale current 1.0 A: $S = \dfrac{1.0 \times 0.10}{5.0 - 1.0} = \dfrac{0.10}{4.0} = 0.025$ Ω, in parallel.

questions.stem_md: An ammeter is made by connecting a shunt of resistance G/49 across a galvanometer of resistance G. What fraction of the total current passes through the galvanometer?
questions.solution_md: The currents divide inversely as the resistances: $\dfrac{I_g}{I_S} = \dfrac{G/49}{G} = \dfrac{1}{49}$, so $\dfrac{I_g}{I} = \dfrac{1}{1 + 49} = \dfrac{1}{50} = 0.020$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A voltmeter of range 0–10 V made from a given galvanometer has a higher resistance than a voltmeter of range 0–1 V made from the same galvanometer.

**Reason (R):** The series resistance needed for a range V is V/Ig − G, which increases with V.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: the meter resistance G + R = V/Ig is proportional to the range, ten times larger for 10 V — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two 4.0 kΩ resistors in series are connected across a 12 V supply of negligible internal resistance. A voltmeter of resistance 4.0 kΩ is connected across one of the resistors. It reads
questions.solution_md: The voltmeter and the resistor in parallel make 2.0 kΩ, in series with 4.0 kΩ: the reading is 12 × 2/6 = 4.0 V, not the 6.0 V present without the meter — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer is converted into an ammeter of range 0–2 A, whose resistance is R. If the same galvanometer is instead converted into an ammeter of range 0–10 A, the resistance of the new ammeter is

options.text_md: 5R
R

questions.solution_md: With $S = G/(n - 1)$ the ammeter resistance is $\dfrac{GS}{G + S} = \dfrac{G}{n}$: five times the range means one fifth of the resistance — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The same galvanometer is used to make an ammeter and a voltmeter. Arrange the galvanometer, the ammeter and the voltmeter in increasing order of resistance and justify the order.

answer.model_answer_md: **Ammeter < galvanometer < voltmeter.** The ammeter is the coil G in **parallel** with a small shunt S, so its resistance GS/(G + S) is **less than S**, and far less than G. The voltmeter is the coil in **series** with a large R, so its resistance G + R is **much more than G**.

questions.solution_md: Parallel lowers, series raises the resistance.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: shunt in parallel lowers, series R raises

questions.stem_md: By mistake, an ammeter of range 0–1.0 A and resistance 0.050 Ω is connected directly across a cell of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.45 Ω. Find the current through the ammeter and comment on the mistake.

answer.model_answer_md: $I = \dfrac{E}{r + R_A} = \dfrac{1.5}{0.45 + 0.050} = 3.0$ A. This is **three times** the full-scale current: the coil and shunt can **overheat** and the meter may be **damaged**. An ammeter has a very low resistance and must always be connected **in series**, never across a source.

marking_scheme.step: Exceeds range: damage; ammeter belongs in series

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer has resistance G and full-scale current Ig. Derive the resistance needed to convert it into (a) an ammeter of range I, (b) a voltmeter of range V, stating how the resistance is connected in each case.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A shunt $S$ is connected **in parallel**. At full scale the coil carries $I_g$ and the shunt $I - I_g$, with the same p.d.: $I_gG = (I - I_g)S$, so $S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g}$ (small).
(b) A resistance $R$ is connected **in series**. Full-scale current $I_g$ must flow when $V$ is applied: $V = I_g(G + R)$, so $R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G$ (large).

questions.solution_md: Equal p.d. in parallel; V = Ig(G + R) in series.

marking_scheme.step: R in series: R = V/Ig − G

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer of resistance 10 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 1.0 mA. Design a two-range voltmeter reading 0–5 V and 0–50 V, using two resistors in series with the galvanometer, and find the resistance of the meter on each range.

answer.model_answer_md:
0–5 V: total $\dfrac{5}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 5000$ Ω, so $R_1 = 5000 - 10 = 4990$ Ω in series; the 5 V terminal is taken after $R_1$.
0–50 V: total $\dfrac{50}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 50000$ Ω, so add $R_2 = 50000 - 5000 = 45000$ Ω after the 5 V terminal.
Meter resistance: 5000 Ω on the 5 V range and 50 000 Ω on the 50 V range.

questions.solution_md: Total resistance V/Ig for each range.

questions.stem_md: (a) A rectangular coil of N turns and area A carries current I in a uniform magnetic field B, its normal making angle θ with B. Show that the net force on the coil is zero and derive the torque acting on it. [3] (b) A coil of 200 turns, 4.0 cm × 2.5 cm, carries 50 mA in a field of 0.80 T. Find its magnetic moment and the torque on it when its plane makes 30° with the field, and state the orientation in which it would come to rest if free to turn. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Take the axis of rotation parallel to the sides of length $l$ (the other sides have length $b$). The forces on opposite sides are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero. The forces on the sides of length $b$ act along the axis and cancel. The sides of length $l$ each feel $F = NIlB$, on parallel lines a distance $b\sin\theta$ apart: a couple of moment $\tau = NIlB \cdot b\sin\theta = NIAB\sin\theta$, or $\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B$ with $\vec m = NI\vec A$ (right-hand rule).

(b) $m = NIA = 200 \times 0.050 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-3} = 0.010$ A m². Plane at $30^\circ$ means $\theta = 60^\circ$: $\tau = 0.010 \times 0.80 \times \sin 60^\circ \approx 6.93 \times 10^{-3}$ N m. It comes to rest with $\vec m$ along $\vec B$, the plane of the coil perpendicular to the field (stable equilibrium).

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain why a small current loop is regarded as a magnetic dipole. [1] (b) An electron revolves with speed v in a circular orbit of radius r. Derive its orbital magnetic moment and show that μ = (e/2mₑ)L, where L is its orbital angular momentum. [2] (c) Using Bohr’s condition L = nh/2π, find the orbital magnetic moment of the electron in the third orbit of hydrogen, and state its direction relative to L. (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Far away its field has the dipole form (axial field $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{x^3}$, N and S faces), and in a uniform field it feels no net force but a torque $\vec m \times \vec B$, like a bar magnet.

(b) Period $T = 2\pi r/v$, so $I = \dfrac{e}{T} = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}$; $\mu = I\pi r^2 = \dfrac{evr}{2}$. With $L = m_evr$, $\mu = \dfrac{e}{2m_e}L$.

(c) $\mu = \dfrac{e}{2m_e}\cdot\dfrac{nh}{2\pi} = n\dfrac{eh}{4\pi m_e} = 3 \times 9.28 \times 10^{-24} \approx 2.78 \times 10^{-23}$ A m². It points opposite to $\vec L$, because the electron is negative.

questions.stem_md: (a) Describe the construction of a moving coil galvanometer and explain the purpose of its radial magnetic field. [2] (b) Show that the deflection of the coil is proportional to the current through it, and define current sensitivity. [1] (c) A galvanometer coil of 50 turns, each of area 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m², is in a radial field of 0.30 T. The restoring torque per unit twist is 1.5 × 10⁻⁸ N m rad⁻¹ and the coil resistance is 25 Ω. Find (i) its current sensitivity, (ii) its voltage sensitivity, (iii) the current that deflects it by 0.15 rad. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A coil of many turns of fine insulated copper wire on a light frame hangs from a phosphor-bronze strip (with a mirror or pointer) between the concave pole pieces of a strong magnet; a soft-iron cylinder sits inside the coil, and a spring below completes the circuit. The concave poles and the core make the field radial, so the plane of the coil always contains B and the deflecting torque is $NIAB$ at every deflection; the core also strengthens B.

(b) $NIAB = c\theta$, so $\theta = \dfrac{NAB}{c}I \propto I$. Current sensitivity is the deflection per unit current, $\theta/I = NAB/c$.

(c)(i) $\dfrac{NAB}{c} = \dfrac{50 \times 3.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.30}{1.5 \times 10^{-8}} = 3.0 \times 10^{5}$ rad A$^{-1}$.
(ii) $\dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{5}}{25} = 1.2 \times 10^{4}$ rad V$^{-1}$.
(iii) $I = \dfrac{0.15}{3.0 \times 10^{5}} = 5.0 \times 10^{-7}$ A.

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain, with a circuit diagram described in words, how a galvanometer is converted into an ammeter, and derive the shunt resistance required. [2] (b) A galvanometer of resistance 45 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 3.0 mA. Find (i) the shunt needed for an ammeter of range 0–2.0 A and the resistance of this ammeter, (ii) the resistance needed for a voltmeter of range 0–24 V and the resistance of this voltmeter. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A small resistance S (the shunt) is connected in parallel with the galvanometer, between the two terminals of the meter. The coil may carry only $I_g$; the rest, $I - I_g$, passes through the shunt at the same p.d.: $I_gG = (I - I_g)S$, so $S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g}$. The combination has a very small resistance and is connected in series.

(b)(i) $S = \dfrac{0.0030 \times 45}{2.0 - 0.0030} = \dfrac{0.135}{1.997} \approx 0.0676$ Ω; ammeter resistance $\dfrac{45 \times 0.0676}{45 + 0.0676} \approx 0.0675$ Ω.
(ii) Total $\dfrac{24}{0.0030} = 8000$ Ω, so $R = 8000 - 45 = 7955$ Ω in series; voltmeter resistance 8000 Ω.

questions.stem_md: A 9.0 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected across a 3.0 kΩ resistor and a 6.0 kΩ resistor in series. (a) Why should an ideal voltmeter have infinite resistance? [1] (b) Find the true p.d. across the 6.0 kΩ resistor, and the reading of a voltmeter of resistance 6.0 kΩ connected across it. [2] (c) Find the least voltmeter resistance for which the reading is within 1% of the true value. A voltmeter of range 0–10 V is made from a galvanometer of full-scale current 50 μA; is it good enough? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A voltmeter is connected in parallel; any current it draws lowers the effective resistance of that part of the circuit and changes the p.d. it is meant to measure. Infinite resistance draws no current.

(b) True p.d. $= 9.0 \times \dfrac{6.0}{9.0} = 6.0$ V. With the meter: $6.0$ kΩ in parallel with 6.0 kΩ is $3.0$ kΩ, so the reading is $9.0 \times \dfrac{3.0}{6.0} = 4.5$ V.

(c) With $R_p$ (the meter in parallel with 6.0 kΩ) in kΩ, the reading must satisfy $9.0 \times \dfrac{R_p}{3.0 + R_p} \ge 0.99 \times 6.0 = 5.94$ V, so $R_p \ge \dfrac{5.94 \times 3.0}{3.06} \approx 5.82$ kΩ, and $R_V = \dfrac{6.0R_p}{6.0 - R_p} \approx 198$ kΩ. The 10 V meter has $\dfrac{10}{50 \times 10^{-6}} = 200$ kΩ, just above 198 kΩ: good enough, only just.
